section_1.title: Prerequisite: The Familiar Vector
section_1.content: Briefly recap the geometric vector we know: arrows in a 2D or 3D coordinate plane. Visualize two arrows (u and v) being added (tip-to-tail) and an arrow being stretched (scalar multiplication). Establish that vectors are usually seen as 'ordered lists of numbers'.
section_1.example: A GPS navigation arrow pointing 'North 5km' and 'East 2km' as a standard coordinate vector.

section_2.title: The Shift: From 'What it is' to 'What it does'
section_2.content: Introduce the concept of abstraction. Explain that a 'Vector Space' is not a collection of arrows, but any set of objects that follow a specific set of rules (axioms). Use an animation of a 'factory machine' where different objects enter, but as long as they interact correctly, the machine works.
section_2.example: Imagine a 'Club' where members don't have to look like arrows; they just have to follow 8 specific club rules (axioms) regarding how they interact with each other and with numbers.

section_3.title: The Core Rules: The Axiom Checklist
section_3.content: Highlight the most critical axioms using icons: Closure (Adding two members stays in the club), Commutativity (Order doesn't matter), and the Identity (The 'Zero' element). Use a graphical split-screen showing these rules applied to arrows on the left and functions on the right.
section_3.example: If you add two 'sad' functions and the result is still a function in your set, you've satisfied the 'Closure' rule.

section_4.title: Case Study: Functions as Vectors
section_4.content: Visualize a sine wave and a cosine wave. Show that you can add them (creating a new wave) and scale them (making the wave taller). Because functions satisfy all 8 axioms, the set of continuous functions is a Vector Space. Use a 'morphing' animation where an arrow slowly transforms into a wave graph.
section_4.example: A synthesizer combining two sound waves (functions) to create a new sound is essentially performing vector addition in a function space.

section_5.title: Visualizing High Dimensions & Subspaces
section_5.content: Introduce the idea that abstract spaces can have infinite dimensions. Use a 'color palette' analogy. Any color can be a 'vector' made of Red, Green, and Blue (basis vectors). Show a 2D plane (subspace) cutting through a 3D space to illustrate where vectors can live.
section_5.example: A digital artist using a 'color picker' device: every color is a vector in the RGB space, and a 'grayscale filter' is a subspace.

section_6.title: Application: Why Abstraction Matters
section_6.content: Explain that by treating things (like images, signals, or signals) as vectors, we can use the same math (Linear Algebra) to solve complex problems like facial recognition or data compression. Show an image being decomposed into a sum of 'basis images'.
section_6.example: A facial recognition robot 'Character' that sees faces not as pictures, but as points (vectors) in a high-dimensional space to find the 'distance' between two people's features.
